newsitem.title: USA: Scientology leader hails French court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Scientology leader hails French court ruling.

text.p: The head of the Church of Scientology on Monday hailed a French court decision that spared a former leader of the group from going to jail on manslaughter and fraud charges because he said the ruling recognised the church as a religious community.

The Rev. Heber Jentzsch said the French appeals court decision was "a dream come true for my church and minority religions. ... Despite political pressure and hysteria promoting a new inquisition, the court has returned to the French tradition of liberty and equality."
He added, "The judges of the appeals court have seen through manipulation by fanatics, self-named and discredited 'experts' whose sole objective is to destroy religious freedom in that country."

The appeals court gave Jean-Jacques Mazier a suspended three-year jail term for manslaughter and fraud after the suicide of a church follower. In October, a lower court had sentenced him to serve 18 months in prison.
The court also acquitted nine of 14 other defendants tied to the organisation who had been sentenced with Mazier on charges ranging from embezzlement to fraud.

At the original trial, Mazier was found guilty of manslaughter and fraud in the 1988 suicide of scientology follower Patrice Vic. The prosecution said Mazier went to the home of Vic, where both Mazier and Vic put pressure on Vic's wife, Nelly, to lend him money to attend a scientology course.
Unable to raise the money, Vic threw himself off his high-rise apartment block in the middle of the night.

At the original trial, prosecutors portrayed the organisation as an enterprise masquerading as a religion, whose chief function was to extort cash from the gullible using abusive high-pressure techniques.

Defence lawyers argued that the church was a legitimate religion and blamed Vic's suicide on long-term depression and alcohol abuse. The trial revolved around whether the Church of Scientology, founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard, was a sect or a religion. As a religion, it could legally ask members for funds.
